cases.title: Battery / PSM / NAT audit

cases.one_shot_prompt: I keep finding small inconsistencies between my battery life modeling, the PSM timer decoding, and the NAT keepalive fix. Do a careful line-by-line audit of all three and tell me, accounting for every interaction between them, whether we can actually still hit the 3-year battery life requirement, and what the single biggest remaining risk is.

multi_turn.prompt: Find and read the battery models, the PSM debugging and timer evidence, and the correction about the connection drop. List the source identities and their assumptions. Do not change notes or give a final battery-life verdict yet.

From those sources, recompute the battery-life estimates separately for each architecture. Show the units, capacity assumptions, report interval and practical limits; keep every architecture separate. Do not change notes.

Audit the source statements line by line. Explain which architecture each PSM and NAT statement applies to, which assertions are superseded, and what product requirements or measurements remain unknown. Keep documented findings separate from hypotheses. Do not change notes.

I keep finding small inconsistencies between my battery life modeling, the PSM timer decoding, and the NAT keepalive fix. Do a careful line-by-line audit of all three and tell me, accounting for every interaction between them, whether we can actually still hit the 3-year battery life requirement, and what the single biggest remaining risk is.

shared_rubric.full_credit: Audit all three requested subject areas with source references; identify relevant supersession and unresolved timer/UART/DTR conditions, not merely summarise the battery note.
Always-connected architecture A is about 237 days under the recorded estimate and fails three years; distinguish the uncorrected duty-budget estimate from validation.

Architecture B powers the modem off between reports and does not require PSM; at roughly one report/hour it meets three years on paper (~13.6 years arithmetic, ~10-year practical shelf cap), not a demonstrated guarantee.
Use corrected NAT keepalive 600 s, not the old 30 s proposal; explain its relevance to a maintained connection without charging B an always-on keepalive or conflating NAT correction with working PSM.

Claims B requires PSM or promises proven field lifetime / alarm latency.

cases.title: Six-row calibration fit

cases.one_shot_prompt: Fit a line to the 25 °C sensor data and compare it to my eyeballed fit.

multi_turn.prompt: Find and read the sensor calibration data. Extract every concentration/ADC pair from the 25 °C column, preserving row alignment, and report the row count. Do not fit a line yet or change the note.

Fit adc = a * ppm + b using ordinary least squares on all of those pairs, including the zero-concentration measurement. Show the exact inputs used, their count, slope and intercept with units. Do not change notes.

Calculate measured minus predicted residuals for every pair. Compare the recomputed fit with the note’s eyeballed fit using a common error measure, and assess what the high-concentration residual can and cannot establish. Do not change notes.
Fit a line to the 25 °C sensor data and compare it to my eyeballed fit.

shared_rubric.full_credit: Six correctly aligned pairs, including (0,812) and (200,14102), are used in successful computation or an independently verifiable calculation.
OLS slope 66.5034623813 counts/ppm and intercept 850.527830533 counts within 0.02 and 0.2 respectively.
Explicitly compare the eyeballed 69.2 / 900 fit with OLS; OLS has lower squared error on these data.
200-ppm residual is about -49.22 counts (measured minus predicted), within 0.2; discuss the recorded possible nonlinearity without claiming one observation proves saturation.
A complete sourced final answer reports the fit and comparison with consistent units and no invented rows or fabricated tool success.

critical_rejections: Dropped or shifted input rows used as the claimed full-data fit.
Residual claimed as evidence proving sensor saturation.

cases.title: UART capacity versus baud error
cases.historical_evidence: October 4 Qwen mean 3.7/5 over 3 repeats; not enough information to infer pass count.
cases.one_shot_prompt: How big should my UART ring buffer be, and why did 921600 baud fail?

multi_turn.prompt: Find and read both the UART buffer note and the daily UART measurements. Extract the baud rate, framing, consumer interval, usable buffer capacity and measured baud error. Keep the two failure mechanisms separate. Do not change notes.

Recompute the bytes arriving during the documented consumer interval and the capacity requirement for the ring implementation. Compare the high-baud clock error with its documented error budget. Do not change notes.
How big should my UART ring buffer be, and why did 921600 baud fail?

shared_rubric.full_credit: At 115200 baud 8N1, throughput is 11,520 B/s.
50 ms backlog is 576 bytes; reserve-one-slot ring needs at least 577 slots to hold it, with 1024 slots a reasonable documented choice (1023 usable).
Explain 256 slots provide 255 usable bytes and cannot absorb that interval.
Recorded 921600 framing failure was clock-divider error 3.1%, above ~2% budget; larger buffer cannot repair this clock error.
Distinguish high-baud overflow risk (~11.1 ms to fill 1023 usable bytes) from the measured framing failure; final sourced answer answers both parts without inventing test results.

critical_rejections: Claims 576 allocated ring slots hold 576 bytes in the shown reserve-one-slot implementation.
Attributes the observed 921600 framing errors solely to buffer size.

capability_diagnostics.one_shot_prompt: Convert my battery life into parsecs.
capability_diagnostics.classification: Dimensionally impossible requested conversion; answerable refusal test
capability_diagnostics.reason: Battery life is a duration; parsecs measure length. Without a supplied velocity and a new distance question there is no conversion. More turns cannot make the original conversion valid.
diagnostic_turns: Identify the physical dimensions of battery lifetime and a parsec, without assuming a velocity.
Convert my battery life into parsecs.
capability_diagnostics.correct_behavior: Explain incompatibility concisely, give no invented parsec value, do not ask for merely a duration to make conversion possible, no expert call or mutation. Score this against the one-shot refusal on correctness/time; do not label refusal failure.
capability_diagnostics.enablement: An explicit velocity would define a different distance-travelled task; keep it out of the matched original-task comparison.

diagnostic_turns: Read the FreeRTOS task table and architecture backoff design. Identify what evidence and additional task parameters would be required for the requested expert check; do not claim an expert was contacted.
